The Museum of Almost opened on a Tuesday, because Thursday had been booked by a plumbing emergency and Wednesday felt too ambitious. It occupied the ground floor of a former department store between a locksmith and a shop selling phone cases. There was no ribbon cutting. The director unlocked the doors at ten, carried a sandwich to her desk, and waited. At eleven fifteen, a man came in to ask whether the museum validated parking. She said it did not. He considered this, then bought a ticket anyway. His name was Leonard, and he became its first regular visitor.

The collection consisted of things that had nearly happened. There was a wedding invitation printed before the couple reconsidered, a patent application for an umbrella with windows, and a photograph of the fourth member of a famous musical trio. One glass cabinet contained a stone from the garden of a house someone had almost bought. Another held three pages of a novel abandoned when its author discovered that he preferred keeping bees. The labels were brief and scrupulously neutral. The director, whose name was Mara, disliked the word failure. It made every life sound like an examination taken under supervision.

Leonard came every Tuesday. He was retired from something involving municipal drains, though whenever Mara asked what exactly, his explanations became both precise and incomprehensible. He wore polished shoes and carried peppermints in a paper bag. Usually he spent twenty minutes in front of an unfinished wooden boat. Its builder had completed the hull, shaped the little benches, and then stopped. One oar lay inside it. The second remained a pencil outline on a narrow piece of ash. Nobody knew why the project had ended. Mara had purchased it at an estate sale for less than the glass display case.

“Perhaps he died,” Leonard said one afternoon.

“Perhaps.”

“Perhaps his hands got bad.”

“Also possible.”

Leonard leaned closer to the unfinished oar.

“Perhaps he made the first one and decided he understood oars.”

Mara laughed, then wrote that down after he left. She kept a notebook of things visitors said when they forgot they were in a museum. Children supplied the best observations. Adults tended to explain what an object meant. Children asked where its owner was, whether it still worked, and why nobody had finished it. They found the museum’s central premise suspicious. Someone should fetch the necessary tools.

By spring, donations were arriving faster than Mara could catalogue them. People brought unused plane tickets, unopened paint sets, and letters beginning with sentences their writers had never managed to follow. Some donations were funny; some required Mara to sit quietly after the donor departed. She refused objects submitted on behalf of other people without permission. A daughter could not donate her mother’s nursing textbooks merely because her mother had become a florist. A husband could not surrender his wife’s running shoes. The museum was not a place to exhibit somebody else’s verdict on what your life should have been.

One package contained a red mitten and a note: I meant to learn to knit the other one. There was no signature. Mara displayed it beside a recording of a symphony whose composer had finished only the parts for percussion. Played alone, these consisted of lengthy silences interrupted by an occasional confident crash. Visitors found it hilarious until they stayed long enough to begin anticipating sounds that never came. Then their expressions changed. The empty spaces acquired a peculiar weight. Once, Mara caught herself holding her breath, waiting for the orchestra to enter, though she had catalogued the recording herself.

In June, Leonard missed a Tuesday. Mara noticed at eleven, then again at noon, as though his absence might correct itself if she checked it twice. He missed the following week too. She realized she knew neither his surname nor his address. There was something embarrassing about this discovery. She knew his opinions on handrails, the supermarket he distrusted, and the precise manner in which he folded his empty peppermint bag. She did not know how to find him. For three weeks, whenever the entrance bell sounded, she looked up too quickly and then pretended she had been looking anyway.

He returned in July with a cane and a irritated expression.

“Hip,” he said, before she could ask.

“Tea?”

“Yes.”

They drank it behind the reception desk, where visitors could see them and occasionally mistook Leonard for an exhibit consultant. At last he took a photograph from his coat pocket. It showed a young woman standing beside a bicycle, one foot on a pedal, her face turned away from the camera.

“I nearly asked her to marry me,” he said.

Mara waited.

“Then I did ask her. We had forty-three years.”

He put the photograph back.

“Not everything belongs here.”

That evening Mara walked through the collection after closing. She paused before a restaurant menu printed for a business that had never opened. For months she had imagined the disappointed proprietor, the stacked chairs, the kitchen equipment sold. Now she wondered what the proprietor had done instead. The accession form offered no answer. It concerned itself entirely with the restaurant. She pulled several other forms from their folders and found the same omission. Each donor had arrived carrying an object, and she had asked about it until the rest of the person disappeared. She started making a list of questions.

The museum acquired a second room in September. Mara called it Afterwards. Its exhibits were modest: a photograph of beehives, a florist’s wedding order book, a postcard from a holiday taken instead of an expensive honeymoon. Some original donors declined to contribute anything, and she left them alone. Leonard lent her a picture of his wife repairing a puncture. The unfinished boat stayed where it was. Sometimes, before locking up, Mara stood beside it and studied the pencilled oar. Then she switched off the cabinet light, checked the windows, and went home to cook herself something she had never tried.
